content:
#1 I’ve decided to bite the bullet, intending to clean up the various messes which have been left for a few years at cycle category and cyclic order. On Mike’s advice in a discussion box in the remarks section at cyclic order, I had a look at the Berger-Moerdijk paper on generalized Reedy categories, and after a bit of work their description of Connes’s category Λ\LambdaΛ became quite clear to me, but they stop short of giving an exposition in the style of “Australian category theory” – not their style, perhaps. I’ve been having a think about all this, and would like to run a few things past you good category theorists.

One observation is that the material on what they call a “crossed RRR-group” (RRR a small category), and its total category, fits pretty neatly into the language of distributive laws. Recall that a category can be regarded as a monad in a bicategory of spans. This means that if I have two categories = monads M:C↛CM: C \nrightarrow CM:C↛C and N:C↛CN: C \nrightarrow CN:C↛C in Span\mathrm{Span}Span, and a distributive law between them, say

θ:N∘M↛M∘N,\theta: N \circ M \nrightarrow M \circ N,θ:N∘M↛M∘N,

then I can form a new category = monad M∘NM \circ NM∘N in the bicategory of spans.

There are many, many examples of this sort of construction. In the context of their paper, their notion of RRR-group is such an example of a distributive law (whose total category is exactly the monad composite). One of the categories is RRR regarded as a span

R0←R1→R0R_0 \leftarrow R_1 \to R_0R0​←R1​→R0​

with its monad structure. Another is a sum of groups GrG_rGr​ indexed by r∈R0r \in R_0r∈R0​, which forms a groupoid G, regarded as a span

R0←∑r∈R0Gr→R0R_0 \leftarrow \sum_{r \in R_0} G_r \to R_0R0​←r∈R0​∑​Gr​→R0​

again with a monad structure. What they call a crossed RRR-group consists precisely (I believe) of two such monads equipped with a distributive law θ:G∘R→R∘G\theta: G \circ R \to R \circ Gθ:G∘R→R∘G between them, where I write composition in Leibnizian order so that G∘RG \circ RG∘R refers to a pullback of a diagram

R1∑rGr↙↘↙↘R0R0R0\begin{matrix} & & R_1 & & & & \sum_r G_r & & \\ & \swarrow & & \searrow & & \swarrow & & \searrow & \\ R_0 & & & & R_0 & & & & R_0 \end{matrix}R0​​↙​R1​​↘​R0​​↙​∑r​Gr​​↘​R0​​

More precisely, θ(α:r→s,g∈Gs)\theta(\alpha: r \to s, g \in G_s)θ(α:r→s,g∈Gs​) would be, in their notation, (α∗(g),g∗(α))(\alpha^\ast(g), g_\ast(\alpha))(α∗(g),g∗​(α)) (lying in the fiber Gr×hom⁡(r,s)G_r \times \hom(r, s)Gr​×hom(r,s) of the span composite R∘GR \circ GR∘G).

Then they describe the Connes cycle category Λ\LambdaΛ as a total category which in our notation would be denoted Δ∘Z\Delta \circ ZΔ∘Z, where the groupoid ZZZ is the sum of all finite cyclic groups ZnZ_nZn​ and Δ:N↛N\Delta: \mathbb{N} \nrightarrow \mathbb{N}Δ:N↛N is the simplex category. They describe the relevant distributive law, modulo the translations above, in terms of a restriction of another distributive law of the form θ:Δ∘P→P∘Δ\theta: \Delta \circ \mathbb{P} \to \mathbb{P} \circ \Deltaθ:Δ∘P→P∘Δ, where P\mathbb{P}P is the groupoid of finite permutations.

It’s at this point where a more conceptual description of what is truly going on seems possible. The idea is that there is a forgetful functor from symmetric monoidal categories to monoidal categories, and another from monoidal categories with a monoid object to monoidal categories. Both of these are (2-)monadic, I believe, and can be described in terms of clubs.

As we know, distributive laws have to do with liftings of monads through monadic functors. In the present case, it seems that the distributive law θ:ΔP→PΔ\theta: \Delta \mathbb{P} \to \mathbb{P} \Deltaθ:ΔP→PΔ has to do with a doctrinal lifting of a club Δ≀N−:MonCat→MonCat\Delta \wr_{\mathbb{N}} -: \mathrm{MonCat} \to {\mathrm{MonCat}}Δ≀N​−:MonCat→MonCat (attached to the doctrine “monoidal categories with a monoid”) through the forgetful functor U:SymMonCat→MonCatU: \mathrm{SymMonCat} \to {\mathrm{MonCat}}U:SymMonCat→MonCat.

It seems to me that there ought to be very conceptual grounds on which to expect the existence of that particular lifting. In any case, I want to think of the category P∘Δ\mathbb{P} \circ \DeltaP∘Δ as just a “symmetrification” of the walking monoid Δ\DeltaΔ, i.e., we’re just applying a change-of-doctrine map to the theory of monoids, from monoidal categories to symmetric monoidal categories.

Similarly, I guess there ought to be a doctrine intermediate between monoidal categories and symmetric monoidal categories, called “cyclic monoidal categories”. I can’t find mention of what I mean through a quick Google search, but whatever they are, I am assuming they can be described as algebras of a club governed by the groupoid ZZZ (just as symmetric monoidal categories are algebras of a club P\mathbb{P}P).

In other words, I am proposing that doctrinally, the Connes cyclic category is the “cyclification” of the walking monoid.

Do people discuss such things, somewhere, somehow?
subject: cyclic monoidal categories (?)

content:
#2 The description of “crossed groups” as distributive laws in Span\mathrm{Span}Span is really nice! I don’t quite follow what’s going on with the rest of it though; how do you get from a distributive law in Span\mathrm{Span}Span to a distributive law of clubs/monads?

To answer your question, this doesn’t ring any bells for me. Although the notion of “cyclic monoidal category” might be related to the notion of “shadow” defined by Kate Ponto. A shadow on a monoidal category VVV is a functor ⟨⟨−⟩⟩:V→T\langle\langle - \rangle\rangle : V \to T⟨⟨−⟩⟩:V→T, for some other category TTT, together with cyclicity isomorphisms ⟨⟨x⊗y⟩⟩≅⟨⟨y⊗x⟩⟩\langle\langle x \otimes y \rangle\rangle \cong \langle\langle y \otimes x \rangle\rangle⟨⟨x⊗y⟩⟩≅⟨⟨y⊗x⟩⟩ satisfying appropriate axioms. Maybe a “cyclic monoidal category” is related to one equipped with a shadow where ⟨⟨−⟩⟩\langle\langle-\rangle\rangle⟨⟨−⟩⟩ is the identity functor, or something?

content:
#3 Sorry if I wasn’t being clear. The basic hope was that if you have an algebraic theory TTT (like the theory of monoids) that is expressible in the doctrine of monoidal categories, let’s say just a one-sorted theory to keep things simple for now, and you want to switch that theory over to a richer doctrine such as the doctrine of symmetric monoidal categories, then it should be given by some simple construction like T∘PT \circ \mathbb{P}T∘P. That is: the one-sorted theory TTT is expressed by a monoidal category called a “pro” (prop minus the p), with underlying set of objects = arities N\mathbb{N}N. As a category, this category = span monad has the form N←A→N\mathbb{N} \leftarrow A \to \mathbb{N}N←A→N. Then you have the free symmetric monoidal category P\mathbb{P}P generated by a single sort, which as a span also has the form N←P→N\mathbb{N} \leftarrow \mathbb{P} \to \mathbb{N}N←P→N, and you want to compose them in some way, in effect adjoining symmetries in a sensible way.

We can put the club stuff on hold, if this seems to be a clearer description of what I was aiming for.

content:
#4 And just to add an additional, hopefully clarifying comment: I meant it when I said (monoidal) algebraic theories TTT, i.e., I mean for the generating operations of TTT to have multiple inputs but just one output, in order for such a simple-minded construction like T∘PT \circ \mathbb{P}T∘P to do its job properly.

The underlying point here is that the relevant distributive law θ:P∘T→T∘P\theta: \mathbb{P} \circ T \to T \circ \mathbb{P}θ:P∘T→T∘P is to be guided purely by naturality considerations. A simple example should get the point across: if we have TTT-operations f:s1⊗…⊗sm→sf: s_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes s_m \to sf:s1​⊗…⊗sm​→s and g:t1⊗…⊗tn→tg: t_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes t_n \to tg:t1​⊗…⊗tn​→t, and we want to think of the theory TTT qua the doctrine of symmetric monoidal categories, then naturality of the symmetry would force the equation

s1⊗…⊗sn⊗t1⊗…⊗tn→f⊗gs⊗t→σstt⊗s      =      s1⊗…⊗sn⊗t1⊗…⊗tn→σs⃗t⃗t1⊗…⊗tn⊗s1⊗…⊗sn→g⊗ft⊗ss_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes s_n \otimes t_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes t_n \stackrel{f \otimes g}{\to} s \otimes t \stackrel{\sigma_{s t}}{\to} t \otimes s\;\;\; = \;\;\; s_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes s_n \otimes t_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes t_n \stackrel{\sigma_{\vec{s} \vec{t}}}{\to} t_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes t_n \otimes s_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes s_n \stackrel{g \otimes f}{\to} t \otimes ss1​⊗…⊗sn​⊗t1​⊗…⊗tn​→f⊗gs⊗t→σst​t⊗s=s1​⊗…⊗sn​⊗t1​⊗…⊗tn​→σst​t1​⊗…⊗tn​⊗s1​⊗…⊗sn​→g⊗ft⊗s

which means the distributive law θ\thetaθ should take the element (f⊗g,σst)(f \otimes g, \sigma_{s t})(f⊗g,σst​) of the span P∘T\mathbb{P} \circ TP∘T to the element (σs⃗,t⃗,g⊗f)(\sigma_{\vec{s},\vec{t}}, g \otimes f)(σs,t​,g⊗f) of T∘PT \circ \mathbb{P}T∘P.

That’s what’s really going on in the description of Λ\LambdaΛ (as found in Berger-Moerdijk). But if you think about it a little, such a simple description of change-of-doctrine applied to a theory, from monoidal categories to symmetric monoidal categories or cyclic monoidal categories, as being just T∘PT \circ \mathbb{P}T∘P or T∘ZT \circ ZT∘Z, wouldn’t be so simple if we were considering more general pros TTT. Here’s another way of putting approximately the same thought: if you have a purely coalgebraic pro TTT, then you’d better use P∘T\mathbb{P} \circ TP∘T instead to switch doctrines (and again let naturality guide the form of the relevant distributive law T∘P→P∘TT \circ \mathbb{P} \to \mathbb{P} \circ TT∘P→P∘T).

(By the way – thanks Mike not just for your response but for pointing me to the paper by you and Kate; I’ll have a look.)

#5 Okay, I get a bit of the idea I think. Normally when I think of lifting a theory TTT from one doctrine D1D_1D1​ to a richer doctrine D2D_2D2​, I think of doing it “universally” so that a T^\hat{T}T^-model in a D2D_2D2​-category is the same as a TTT-model in its underlying D1D_1D1​-category. That sort of lifting doesn’t require any extra structure on TTT, it just exists universally. Are you saying we can instead choose some extra structure on TTT (namely, a distributive law) to lift it to D2D_2D2​ in a different (hence not universal) way?

This also reminds me of section 6.7 (page 169) of HOHC on “change of shape” morphisms between generalized multicategories, which are also constructed as certain composites in bicategories of spans.

content:
#6 No, I didn’t think I was saying that. I thought what I was doing just now was giving a simple direct construction of what you call T^\hat{T}T^ in terms of TTT, at least when TTT is an algebraic theory in D1D_1D1​ = doctrine of monoidal categories, and D2D_2D2​ is something like the doctrine of symmetric monoidal categories, or braided monoidal categories, or cartesian categories… or indeed cyclic monoidal categories (modeled after your “shadows”).

The thread started off being about the cyclic category Λ\LambdaΛ, and the description I’m putting forth, which I’ve never seen before, is that it is the “theory of monoids within the doctrine of cyclic monoidal categories”, i.e., it classifies monoids within this doctrine: if CCC is a cyclic monoidal category, then the category of cyclic monoidal functors Λ→C\Lambda \to CΛ→C is equivalent to the category of monoids in CCC. Parallel to the way that Δ\DeltaΔ classifies monoids within the doctrine of monoidal categories. Moreover, I am suggesting in #3 and #4 that this abstract conceptual description leads directly to its explicit concrete description, as Δ∘Z\Delta \circ ZΔ∘Z. If someone asks you how to write down the distributive law Z∘Δ→Δ∘ZZ \circ \Delta \to \Delta \circ ZZ∘Δ→Δ∘Z used in this description, you can answer that it’s just the obvious law you need in order to ensure that the cyclic monoidal structure constraints M⊗N→N⊗MM \otimes N \to N \otimes MM⊗N→N⊗M (which come from ZZZ, the groupoid of finite cyclic permutations) do in fact behave as natural transformations when viewed in Δ∘Z\Delta \circ ZΔ∘Z, which is what I was trying to explain in #4 via an example.

Thanks for your feedback, and please let me know if I’m not being clear.

content:
#8 Yes, that is what I’m hoping to be able to prove, restricting for now to D1D_1D1​ = doctrine of monoidal categories, and D2D_2D2​ a doctrine of somewhat more enriched monoidal type (symmetric, braided, cyclic, etc.), since I’m not quite sure what shape a more general theorem would have. And also with the proviso that a D1D_1D1​-theory means generated from operations each having a single output sort, and that equations declared in the theory are between terms of the same type s1⊗…⊗sn→ts_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes s_n \to ts1​⊗…⊗sn​→t, again with single output sort ttt. (The last is probably already understood, but I’m playing it safe here; it would ruin the hoped-for theorem if we allowed D1D_1D1​-equations to occur between terms with output T=t1⊗…⊗tmT = t_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes t_mT=t1​⊗…⊗tm​ that don’t come about by tensoring together mmm equations of the type I just described.)

Not to belabor the point, but in the case where D2D_2D2​ is symmetric monoidal categories, the idea is to adjoin symmetry isomorphisms to the D1D_1D1​-theory, and be able to rewrite a map ϕ∘(f1⊗…⊗fm)\phi \circ (f_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes f_m)ϕ∘(f1​⊗…⊗fm​) where ϕ\phiϕ is a symmetry isomorphism t1⊗…⊗tm→tσ(1)⊗…tσ(m)t_1 \otimes \ldots \otimes t_m \to t_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \ldots t_{\sigma(m)}t1​⊗…⊗tm​→tσ(1)​⊗…tσ(m)​ as (fσ(1)⊗…⊗fσ(m))∘ϕ′(f_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \ldots \otimes f_{\sigma(m)}) \circ \phi'(fσ(1)​⊗…⊗fσ(m)​)∘ϕ′ where ϕ′\phi'ϕ′ is another symmetry isomorphism. Seems simple enough, right? String-diagrammatically, push symmetry isomorphisms to the top, by a kind of “combing” procedure. That dictates the form of the distributive law: θ(ϕ,f1⊗…⊗fm)=(fσ(1)⊗…⊗fσ(m),ϕ′)\theta(\phi, f_1\otimes \ldots \otimes f_m) = (f_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \ldots \otimes f_{\sigma(m)}, \phi')θ(ϕ,f1​⊗…⊗fm​)=(fσ(1)​⊗…⊗fσ(m)​,ϕ′).

Then an ordinary multicategory XXX, i.e. a (co-unary) D1D_1D1​-theory, is a span X0←X1→D1X0X_0 \leftarrow X_1 \to D_1 X_0X0​←X1​→D1​X0​ with a monad structure in D1D_1D1​-Span\mathrm{Span}Span.
